kernels.definition: Rhythm (from Greek ῥυθμός, rhythmos, "any regular recurring motion, symmetry") generally means a "movement marked by the regulated succession of strong and weak elements, or of opposite or different conditions".

mcItems.q: Which choice best matches what musical form describes in a composition?
op: The overall structure of the piece
The number of chords in a phrase
The exact pitch pattern of a scale
The loudness level of each section
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the overall structure of the piece. A common misconception is to treat form as the chord count or another single surface feature, but form is the larger organization that unfolds over time; it results from the interaction of the musical elements, not just one of them.

mcItems.q: In notation for a musical form, what do lowercase letters such as a and b usually indicate?
op: Subdivisions of a larger unit
Two sections of equal length
A harmonic cadence pattern
A repeated rhythmic ratio
mcItems.ex: Lowercase letters mark subdivisions of each large musical unit. The tempting mistake is to read them as naming the piece’s two main parts, but two sections of about equal length describes binary form, not the lettering used for subdivisions.

keyTerms.df: The overall structure of a musical composition or performance.
keyTerms.eg: A movement can be analyzed by how its sections are arranged and developed over time.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as a chord progression.
keyTerms.cx: Chord progression is only one kind of evidence; form is the larger structural organization that can include harmony, melody, and rhythm.

keyTerms.df: A design with two sections that are about equal in length.
keyTerms.eg: A short piece divided into two balanced parts can be described this way.
keyTerms.mi: Any time a score uses lowercase letters, it must be binary form.
keyTerms.cx: Lowercase letters can mark subdivisions within a larger unit; they do not by themselves prove a two-section design.

mcItems.q: A student labels a sonority built from three notes stacked in thirds as a seventh chord because it sounds harmonically complete. What is the best correction?
op: It is a triad, since three notes can be stacked vertically in thirds.
It is a seventh chord, since every stacked sonority contains a seventh.
It is an inversion of a seventh chord, since it has three notes.
It is not a chord, since thirds only describe melody.
mcItems.ex: The best correction is that three notes stacked in thirds form a triad. The tempting misconception is to treat any harmonically full-sounding sonority as a seventh chord, but a seventh chord requires a triad plus an added note a seventh above the root.

mcItems.q: A composer wants a sonority that adds instability and can push the music toward motion in a specific direction. Which chord type best matches that description?
op: A triad, because three notes stacked in thirds are the most directional.
A seventh chord, because the added seventh can destabilize the triad.
A unison, because one pitch can imply any harmonic goal.
A scale, because stepwise order creates chordal tension.
mcItems.ex: A seventh chord best matches that description because the added seventh can destabilize the triad and help emphasize motion in a chosen direction.
